references.text: The preceding verse provides the context: John the Baptist sends two of his disciples to Jesus with exactly this question. Verse 20 repeats the question when they arrive.
The people wondered if John himself was the Messiah, but John pointed forward to the one who would come after him – 'the one who comes' – the same expression used in 7:20.
The parallel passage in Matthew where John the Baptist, from prison, sends a message to Jesus with the same question: 'Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?'
John the Baptist speaks of 'the one who comes after me' – the expression 'the one who comes' (ὁ ἐρχόμενος) is central and directly linked to the messianic expectation in the question in Luke 7:20.
'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord' – the messianic title 'he who comes' has its background in this psalm and is the same expression used by John's disciples.
John the Baptist testifies about 'the one who comes after me', which connects to the messianic expectation underlying the question in Luke 7:20.
The people identify Jesus as 'the prophet who is to come into the world' – the same messianic expectation of 'the one who comes' as in Luke 7:20.
Jacob's blessing that 'Shiloh shall come' is one of the early messianic prophecies about the coming one, forming the background for the expectation of 'the one who comes'.

'Behold, I send my messenger ... and suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple' – Malachi's prophecy about the coming Lord is the background for John's question whether Jesus is the expected one.
Jesus' answer to the question asked in verse 20: He does not answer directly but points to his deeds as signs that he is the one who was to come, in line with Isaiah's messianic prophecies.

The prophecy that God himself will come and open the eyes of the blind, make the deaf hear, and cause the lame to leap – the messianic signs Jesus points to in answer to the question from John's disciples.
